q: You declare a variable with var inside an if block and access it outside. It works. Why?
options: if blocks don't create scope in JS
var hoists to the file level
explain: var ignores block boundaries like if and for. It only respects function scope. Use let or const for block-scoped behavior.

q: Your function logs undefined before a var variable is assigned. What is happening?
options: var is hoisted but not its value
You need let for logging to work
explain: var declarations are hoisted to the top of their scope but initialized as undefined. The value only exists after the assignment line runs.

q: 0 == false returns true but 0 === false returns false. Why?
options: == is broken and should never be used
== checks value and type, === checks value only
== coerces types before comparing, === does not
false is stored as 0 so they are always equal
explain: == converts both values to the same type before comparing. === never coerces — it checks value and type strictly.

q: typeof null returns 'object'. Your teammate says your code has a bug. Do they?
options: Yes — null must be reassigned first
No — it's a known historical JS bug
No — null is an object by design
explain: typeof null returning 'object' is a preserved bug from JS's original implementation. To check for null use strict equality: value === null.

q: You sort an array of numbers and 10 appears before 2. What went wrong?
options: Arrays over 9 items need a different method
sort() converts to strings and sorts alphabetically
You need to reverse before sorting
explain: sort() converts elements to strings by default. '10' comes before '2' alphabetically. Pass a comparator to sort numerically: array.sort((a, b) => a - b).

q: You copy an object to a new variable, change a property, and the original changes too. Why?
options: Objects are immutable so something else is wrong
Both variables point to the same object in memory
JS automatically syncs objects with matching properties
explain: Objects are assigned by reference not by value. Both variables point to the same memory location so changes through either variable affect the same object.

q: Your arrow function with curly braces returns undefined despite having a return statement. Why?
options: Curly braces require an explicit return keyword
Arrow functions only work with implicit returns
explain: Curly braces create a block body that requires an explicit return. Without curly braces the expression is returned implicitly.

q: You refactor an object method from a regular function to an arrow function and this breaks. Why?
options: Arrow functions don't support this at all
Arrow functions inherit this from their lexical scope
You need to call .bind(this) on arrow functions
this only works inside class methods
explain: Arrow functions don't have their own this — they inherit it from the surrounding scope. As object methods they pick up this from outside the object, not from the object itself.

q: What is the cleanest way to combine two arrays in modern JavaScript?
explain: The spread operator creates a new array with all elements from both. arr1.push(arr2) adds the second array as a nested element, not merged.

q: Accessing a let variable before its declaration throws a ReferenceError. var just logs undefined. Why?
options: let is not hoisted, var is fully hoisted
let stays in a Temporal Dead Zone until its declaration
ReferenceError means let doesn't exist in older JS
var is the only declaration that works before its line
explain: Both are hoisted but differently. var initializes as undefined. let sits in a Temporal Dead Zone and throws if accessed before its declaration line.

q: You need to check if a value is NaN. You try value === NaN and it always returns false. Why?
options: NaN requires double equals to compare
NaN is not equal to anything including itself
You need to convert to string first
explain: NaN is the only value in JS that is not equal to itself. Use Number.isNaN(value) to check for NaN correctly.

q: What is the difference between null and undefined in JavaScript?
options: They are identical, just different syntax
null means no value assigned, undefined means intentionally empty
undefined is uninitialized, null is intentionally set to no value
null is for objects, undefined is for primitives
explain: undefined means a variable was declared but never assigned. null is explicitly assigned by the developer to represent the absence of a value.

q: You want to extract name and age from a user object into separate variables. What is the cleanest way?
options: const name = user.name; const age = user.age
explain: Destructuring lets you extract multiple properties in one line. const { name, age } = user is the modern idiomatic approach.

q: You want the first item of an array without knowing its name. What is the cleanest approach?
explain: Array destructuring lets you extract items by position. const [first] = array grabs the first element cleanly. shift() also works but mutates the original array.

q: Your colleague uses var inside a for loop and the variable leaks outside. What should they use instead?
options: let — it is block-scoped and stays inside the loop
function — wrap the loop in a function
explain: let is block-scoped and stays within the for loop. var leaks out because it is function-scoped. Use let for loop counters that should not exist outside the loop.

q: You use .map() on an array but forget to return inside the callback. Every element becomes undefined. Why?
options: map() requires a separate return array
The callback returned undefined so map used that as the value
map() only works on string arrays
explain: map() builds a new array from whatever each callback returns. If the callback has no return statement it returns undefined, so the new array is full of undefineds.

q: What does the spread operator do when used with an object?
options: Converts the object to an array
Creates a deep clone of the object
Copies the object's own enumerable properties into a new object
explain: The spread operator does a shallow copy — it copies top-level properties. Nested objects are still referenced not cloned.

q: You want to run code after a 2 second delay. Which method do you use?
explain: setTimeout runs a function once after a delay in milliseconds. setInterval would run it repeatedly every 2 seconds.

q: You need to check if an array includes a specific value. What is the cleanest way?
explain: array.includes() returns true or false. contains() and has() don't exist on arrays. find() returns the element itself not a boolean.

q: You want to convert a string '42' to a number. What are valid ways?
explain: Number() and the unary plus operator both convert strings to numbers. parseInt and parseFloat also work but Number() is the cleanest for simple cases.

q: You want to loop over an array and run a function for each item without creating a new array. Which method do you use?
explain: forEach runs a function for each item and returns nothing. map creates a new array. Use forEach when you only need the side effect not a transformed result.

q: You want to remove duplicate values from an array. What is the quickest modern approach?
explain: Set only stores unique values. Spreading it back into an array gives you a deduplicated version in one line. The other options don't exist in JS.

q: You want to get the last item of an array without knowing its length. What is the cleanest way?
explain: Arrays are zero-indexed so the last item is at length minus 1. array[array.length] would be undefined. array.last() doesn't exist natively.

q: You want to check if a variable is an array. What is the reliable way?
explain: typeof returns 'object' for arrays so it's useless here. Array.isArray() is the correct and reliable method.

q: You need to add a property to an existing object. What is the correct way?
explain: You can add properties directly using dot notation or bracket notation. push() is for arrays. addProperty() and Object.add() don't exist.
